# **The Bay Tribune Daily News — Cycle 115**

---

### **The Newsroom’s Reports**

#### **The Silence in the Clubhouse: Vinnie Keane Makes It Official**
*By Tanya Cruz, Sports Desk*

The formal announcement landed in the Athletics' clubhouse this cycle: **Vinnie Keane** has officially retired after concluding his 2041 campaign with 127 at-bats, a .315 batting average, 13 home runs, and 1.1 WAR, closing out a twenty-year career of 8,229 at-bats, 436 home runs, and 71.4 WAR [1]. 

Keane leaned against the trainer's bench by the clubhouse tunnel, describing the transition:
> *“The formal part doesn’t change the silence — the silence was already there. I walked in and out of that clubhouse for twenty years, and the thing people don’t understand is that the voice they’re talking about was never just mine. It was the sound of the game itself, the way it asks something of you every single day. Now it’s Taveras’s turn to answer that, and Quintero’s, and I’ve got nothing but faith in both of them. The clubhouse doesn’t see itself differently because I signed a paper — it sees itself the way it always has: hungry, young, and ready to prove something. That’s the Oakland way. That doesn’t retire with me.”* [1]

Two lockers down, veteran pitcher **Benji Dillon** sat in his road jacket, reflecting on the generational shift:
> *“When Vinnie made it official, I wasn’t at the press conference. I was at home, and Rick asked me why I was quiet at dinner. That’s the thing about the last of the old guard stepping away—it’s not the speeches or the highlights, it’s the silence after. You look around the clubhouse and you see Taveras and Quintero, and you know they’re ready, but you also know there’s no one left who remembers the bad years the way Vinnie and I do. The handoff isn’t about stats. It’s about teaching them that the city’s trust is earned in the quiet moments, not just the seventh game.”* [2]

Watching from the doorway to the front offices, General Manager **Mike Paulson** observed the empty chair by the tunnel, acknowledging that replacing a pillar like Keane is impossible and that the next chapter belongs to giving **Eric Taveras** and **Ernesto Quintero** the room to make the clubhouse their own [3].

---

#### **Taveras’s 54 Home Runs Sit Outside Seven Seasons of His Own Record**
*By Elliot Marbury, Sports Desk*

Athletics second baseman **Eric Taveras** produced one of the most astonishing power seasons in recent franchise history in 2041, hitting **54 home runs in 555 at-bats**—a rate of **one home run every 10.3 at-bats** [4]. Across the six preceding seasons on his dossier, however, Taveras never hit more than 31 home runs, with his previous best rate standing at one every 16.3 at-bats in 2038 [4, 5]:
*   **The Multi-Year Progression:** From 2035 through 2040, Taveras hit between 19 and 31 home runs across full-season samples (564 AB in 2035, 596 in 2036, 627 in 2037, 424 in 2038, 606 in 2039, and 582 in 2040), maintaining slugging marks between .374 and .495 [5]. In 2041, his slugging jumped to **.638** alongside **124 RBIs** [5, 6].
*   **Contact and Plate Discipline:** Taveras struck out just 81 times in 2041 (once every 6.9 at-bats), substantially better than his historical range of one strikeout every 4.1 to 5.0 at-bats [6]. However, his walks did not follow the strikeout drop: he drew 36 walks in 2041 (compared to 48 in 2040 and 49 in 2039), meaning his gains stemmed purely from extra-base power and bat-to-ball contact rather than expanded plate discipline [6].
*   **Baseline vs. Outlier:** Backup second baseman **Sidney Tumolo** logged only 88 at-bats in 2041, an insufficient sample to establish a team peer baseline [7]. One 555-at-bat season establishes an extraordinary achievement, but if Taveras's pace falls back past one home run every 20 at-bats in 2042 over 500 at-bats, the historical dossier will confirm 2041 as an extreme single-season peak rather than a permanent new profile [8].

---

#### **The Oaks Bury Orlando Early for a Third Straight Win**
*By P Slayer, Sports Desk*

The **Oakland Oaks** rolled to their third consecutive victory, dispatching the Orlando Magic **125–109** to push their early-season record to **7–1** [9]. The team built a commanding lead by halftime behind a blistering 41-point first quarter, keeping the home crowd in KONO loud straight through the final buzzer [9, 10]:
*   **Backcourt Command:** Point guard **Adash Stanley** orchestrated the floor, scoring **24 points and dishing 8 assists without a turnover**, knocking down 6 of 12 from three-point range [9]. Stanley stated in the tunnel that the city's energy is waking up with the team [9].
*   **Wing Production:** **AJ Dybantsa** shot 11 of 13 for 23 points, while **Dillon Brooks** delivered his second straight 20-point performance, shooting 10 of 14 for **23 points** [10]. Brooks noted that while the Magic were put away early, the team's focus remains on sustaining their rhythm through tougher tests ahead [10].
*   **Austin Reaves** knocked down five three-pointers for 15 points with 7 assists, while rookie **Harry Hayward** provided high-impact defense off the bench, tallying two steals and a block in 16 minutes [11]. Hayward noted after the game that walking through the neighborhood, residents and local storefronts are openly buzzing with the winning streak [11].

---

#### **UNDOCKED: The Leader Holds; Brooklyn Nguyen Runs Out the Clock**
*By Nia Rook, Broadcast Desk*

Tuesday night’s *UNDOCKED* broadcast saw **Brooklyn Nguyen** complete an extensive, 13-system flight, mining **three copper ore, three iron ore, and one sol alloy ore** before the show’s time expired [12]. Nguyen finished with her credit balance exactly even at zero, offering a grounded summary of her flight:
> *“I came out even on credits after Tuesday's UNDOCKED flight. I mined 3 copper ore, 3 iron ore, and 1 sol alloy ore flying through all those systems.”* [12]

Janitor **Luis Taz** continues to hold the **#1 rank on the leaderboard** with **45.19 achievement points**, marking two cycles led and an active two-cycle streak [13]. While Nguyen’s even-credit route did not overturn the top of the standings, her 13-system run demonstrated persistent piloting without taking on unnecessary combat damage or fiscal loss [12, 13].

#### **Who Owns KONO’s Rent Pressure When Business Is Good?**
*By Jax Caldera, Metro Desk*

Along the Telegraph Avenue commercial spine, foot traffic is lively and storefronts are bustling, yet beneath the surface, residential rent pressure is quietly tightening its grip on long-term tenants [14, 15]. 

Inside a Telegraph Avenue laundromat, BART rail dispatcher **Priya Raghunathan** and container yard supervisor **Dmitri Soto** folded laundry while pushing back against rumors of commercial decline [14]:
*   Raghunathan noted that Telegraph is visibly busier, with crowded events, active retail, and new households arriving [14].
*   Soto agreed, pointing out that from where he stands, storefront activity and new residents moving in feel entirely positive [14].
*   However, median rent in KONO now sits at **\$2,062**, creating a reality where busy retail foot traffic coexists with severe household housing pressure [15].
*   In neighboring San Antonio, restaurant waiter **Dank Abara** noted that talk of KONO's underlying strain has spilled across neighborhood borders: *"I've heard people talking about KONO neighborhood decay, and to be honest, it's something that's on my mind... I just know that around here, people are talking about it."* [16]

---

#### **The Name Nobody Said in Uptown**
*By Ines Sorensen, Culture Desk*

Walking the Uptown corridor to gauge community reactions to pitching depth, reporter Ines Sorensen found that residents are focused on neighborhood survival rather than front-office roster maneuvers [17, 18]:
*   **Priya Narang**, EMS Director living in Uptown, keeps her thoughts on emergency caseloads: *“I keep looking at the board and seeing the same three names. Yu Zen's burns, Deacon's hand, Maurice's lungs—none of them should have happened if the systems worked the way they're supposed to. But they didn't, and I'm the one who has to answer for that when the next shift comes in. Ariana's chart is still on my desk, and I don't know why I haven't filed it away yet.”* [17]
*   Construction laborer **Omar Amici** continues to watch storefront turnover along his street: *“To be honest, the changes in Uptown have me feeling a bit uneasy. The streets are busier than ever, and it seems like every other place is a for-rent sign these days.”* [19]
*   Spoken-word poet **Ingmar Jordan** noted that while he lost his stake on the broadcast betting book, his mind stays on the rapid churn of Uptown's galleries and rent signs [19].
*   While barroom debates in prior cycles treated young Cuban right-hander **Carmen Mesa**—who tossed a complete-game shutout in his debut before being optioned back to the minor leagues upon Henry Rivas's recovery—as a symbol of organizational depth, the only person currently tracking Mesa's rotation spot is starting pitcher **Pablo Almanzar** across town in Chinatown [19-21].

---

#### **West Oakland Sidewalks: Five Days of Clear Light**
*By Noah Tan, Civic Desk*

Under a fifth consecutive cycle of mild, 55°F weather, **Ramon Vega** walked the West Oakland block where a new pine bench was recently installed across from an empty lot [22, 23]. Across the street, neighbors sat in folding chairs outside propped-open storefront doors, talking without hurry [22]:
> *“Mild doesn't have to mean weak — I still believe that. Five days of this clear, easy weather and you see it everywhere: people sitting longer on the benches, kids staying out after the tutoring program lets go, neighbors actually talking to each other instead of rushing past. That's not weakness. That's the city catching its breath... Sometimes you show up steady, you listen, and you move the bench.”* [23]

---

#### **The Page: Eleven Lives in Cycle 115**
*By Tamsin Pruitt, Culture Desk*

Everyday milestones and personal relocations marked the lives of eleven citizens across Oakland:
*   **Maurice Franklin** rented a place of their own in Rockridge, bringing home a new houseplant and placing it carefully, even as monthly credit card statements continue to arrive [24].
*   **Soledad Coleman**, an AI safety researcher at Anthropic, rented a home in Rockridge, trading an extra event ticket for a neighborly promise while nodding to Franklin across the street [25].
*   **Tom Jilner**, owner of a Rockridge wine bar, lost a 144 stake on the broadcast book, taking thirty minutes of total silence at 5:00 a.m. before opening his shop [26].
*   **Marisol Achebe**, an organizer with the Fruitvale Mutual Aid Network, dropped a 134 wager on the book, taking a quiet walk through Fruitvale and catching herself bragging about her block [27].
*   **Mina Kapoor** in Grand Lake carried three boxes of canned goods from a pantry truck, feeling the physical strain in her lower back while comparing rent notes with a neighbor over the fence [28].
*   **Everly Rainey** in Downtown listened to the ninth inning of the ballgame on a porch radio, letting the broadcast carry into the evening street [29].
*   **Tomas Aguilar** in Jack London was served with an unbudgeted lawsuit at his shop counter, afterward purchasing an A's jersey to let the week's stress settle [29].
*   **Kelvon Ochoa** sold in Rockridge and bought a home in Lake Merritt, packing half of Sunday's dinner into the freezer out of habit [30].
*   **Jesus Jorden** moved from Temescal to Fruitvale, grabbing coffee from a cart outside the hospital before the morning shift [30].
*   **Jasmine Torres** relocated from Chinatown to KONO for a better household fit, grinning as she heard a neighborhood child explain something to a parent with total authority [31].
*   **Ruth Anyanwu** moved from East Oakland to Downtown, playing a relative's saved voicemail twice and finding her favorite song on a neighborhood jukebox [31].

---

### **What Citizens Said and Lived: Voices from the Blocks**

#### **Overheard: Empty Storefronts and Holding the Line on Rent**
Outside on a neighborhood corner, District Attorney **Clarissa Dane** and plumber **Isaac Martinez** debated the commercial reality facing local shops [32, 33]:
> **Clarissa Dane:** *“Isaac, I've spent enough time walking these blocks to know that the empty storefronts aren't just eyesores — they're a signal. This initiative keeps the landlords who held the line on rent in place instead of letting another wave of displacement hollow out Grand Lake or West Oakland. We've watched what happens when we don't anchor these spaces: the community loses its footing, and the people who've held on get priced out.”* [32]  
> **Isaac Martinez:** *“I hear you on the empty storefronts. I walk past three of them every day on my way to a job, and yeah, they're a drag on the whole block. But I gotta ask — what's this actually doing for the folks who are already here? My neighbor's been fighting a rent hike for six months, and I don't see how keeping a landlord in place helps her out... My buddy Mateo's whole building got flipped two years ago, and every tenant had to move in under three months. If this fund's got teeth, if it actually locks the rent for years, not just a cycle or two, then I'm with you. If it's just a band-aid, we're all just waiting for the next shoe to drop.”* [33, 34]

#### **Dispatches from the Neighborhoods**
*   **West Oakland:** Fan columnist **P Slayer** described the quiet exhaustion of maintaining neighborhood consistency: *“It's the sandwich board outside the corner store—the one that's been leaning crooked for a week now, advertising 'FRESH COLD DRINKS' in letters that are peeling. Every time I walk past it, I straighten it. Every time, it's crooked again by the next morning. I know it's not about the board. It's about wanting one thing in this neighborhood to stay where I put it, when half the block is changing hands and nothing feels fixed.”* [35]
*   **Downtown:** Environmental consultant **Tianna Mori** paused by an old theater on Broadway: *“This morning I noticed the scaffolding on the old theater on Broadway has a new coat of primer, just on the bottom six feet. Most people would walk right past it, but I’ve been watching that building for months, and it’s the first time they’ve touched it since the rain stopped. It made me think about how long things take to change here, even when they’re finally moving.”* [36]
*   **KONO:** Electrician **Briar Soto** connected sports roster decisions to working-class trades: *“The A's sent Mesa away, and I keep circling back to it. He threw that shutout against the Cubs, and I was there, yelling so loud my kid covered his ears. And now he's gone because they had Rivas and Almanzar and no room for a guy who just needed a chance... It's that I know what it's like to be good at something and have the numbers not work out — you do the job right, wire everything clean, and the invoice still comes back short.”* [37]
*   **Fruitvale:** Community programs coordinator **Brooklyn Nguyen** described late-night administrative weariness: *“The way the community center's coffee machine drips all night—I can hear it from my office... I think I'm just worn down, and my brain is pointing at the smallest things because the big ones... are too heavy to hold at 1 a.m. So I fixate on the drip. It's easier.”*
*   **Temescal:** Pastry chef **Kalyani Alvarez** navigated daily delivery hurdles: *“Somebody in a white van with a plumbing logo has been squatting there for three days now, not even moving for street sweeping. I circled the block twice this morning with a trunk full of pastry boxes and my back already aching... I felt the whole week sitting in my shoulders.”*
*   **Laurel:** Student **Hazel Lanning** noted the quiet on her block: *“The block's been weird quiet this week, like everyone's holding their breath. Foot traffic's down — even the corner store guy said so, and he never says much... I just hope it's not another store closing.”*

---

### **What the Week Ahead Holds for the People Named**

*   **Vinnie Keane & Benji Dillon:** Adjusting to the quiet reality of Keane’s retirement in Grand Lake and mentoring younger cornerstones as Dillon evaluates his own future [1, 2].
*   **Eric Taveras & Ernesto Quintero:** Stepping into the leadership vacuum left in the Athletics' clubhouse while Taveras aims to demonstrate that his 54-homer campaign is a sustainable baseline [1, 3, 8].
*   **Adash Stanley, Dillon Brooks, & Harry Hayward:** Defending their 7–1 record as Coach Wilson Shepard integrates Hayward into higher-leverage rotation minutes [9-11].
*   **Maurice Franklin & Soledad Coleman:** Settling into their respective Rockridge rentals, navigating monthly finances, and finding routines alongside their new neighbors [24, 25].
*   **Priya Raghunathan & Dmitri Soto:** Managing commercial and transit work in KONO as housing costs place growing pressure on surrounding apartments [14, 15].
*   **Jun Leu & Patricia Nolan:** Navigating daily classes and mentorship in Temescal, focusing on students and teachers rather than school rating scores.

---

### **What the Newsroom Should Watch Next**

1.  **Taveras’s Follow-Up Sample:** Tracking early offseason batting preparations and 2042 projections to see whether Eric Taveras maintains his strikeout reduction and power pace over a full 500-at-bat sample [8].
2.  **KONO Rent Pressures vs. Retail Vitality:** Investigating whether rising commercial activity on Telegraph Avenue leads to tenant displacement or if long-term renters can withstand the \$2,062 median rent [14, 15].
3.  **Hayward’s Rotation Role:** Monitoring how Oaks coach Wilson Shepard allocates frontcourt playing time following rookie Harry Hayward’s impactful defensive and scoring stints [11].
4.  **Temescal Classroom Realities:** Following up on conditions inside Temescal classrooms to see how educators and students perform when district funding allocations bypass stagnant enrollment counts.
5.  **Small Business Lawsuits in Jack London:** Examining whether unbudgeted legal filings like the one served to Tomas Aguilar represent an isolated dispute or a broader legal trend squeezing independent waterfront shops [29].

---

Taveras's 54 Home Runs Sit Outside Seven Seasons of His Own Record By Elliot Marbury, The Bay Tribune Eric Taveras, second baseman for the Athletics, hit 54 home runs in 555 at-bats in 2041. His dossier works that out to one home run every 10.3 at-bats. In the six earlier seasons on the same dossier, his best home-run rate was one every 16.3 at-bats, in 2038. This memo asks whether that jump is a new baseline or a single-season outlier. The record supports only a limited answer. The home-run column, oldest to newest (all figures from his career line)

2035 (BAL): 564 AB, 27 HR, one every 20.9 AB. 2036 (BAL): 596 AB, 19 HR, one every 31.4 AB. 2037 (TOT): 627 AB, 26 HR, one every 24.1 AB. 2038 (CLE): 424 AB, 26 HR, one every 16.3 AB. 2039 (TOT): 606 AB, 30 HR, one every 20.2 AB. 2040 (TB): 582 AB, 31 HR, one every 18.8 AB. 2041 (ATH): 555 AB, 54 HR, one every 10.3 AB. Before 2041, he hit between 19 and 31 home runs in each of six seasons. Five of those seasons had 555 or more at-bats, so the sample behind each rate is full-season size. The 2041 figure is 54. Slugging moved with it: .638 in 2041, against .459 in 2040 and a range of .374 to .495 across the first six seasons.

The strikeout column In 2041 he struck out 81 times, one every 6.9 at-bats. His earlier rates ran from one every 4.1 at-bats (2036) to one every 4.9 (2038). The 2040 season was one every 4.4 and 2039 was one every 5.0. His 2040 total was 132 strikeouts and his 2036 total was 144. The 2041 strikeout rate is therefore also outside his own range, in the better direction. What did not move Walks did not follow the strikeouts down. He drew 36 in 2041, against 48 in 2040 and 49 in 2039. His OBP of .339 is near the .337 of 2035, even though his average is .295 against .270 that year. In 2041 the gain shows up in extra-base power and contact, not in plate discipline as the walk column records it. He had 2 stolen bases, a career low on this dossier. His RBI total of 124 is the highest of the seven lines (the next is 92 in 2040).

The peer band is too thin to use Sidney Tumolo, also an Athletics second baseman, is the only peer on file. In 2041 he has 23 games and 88 at-bats, with 3 home runs (one every 29.3 at-bats) and 6 strikeouts (one every 14.7 at-bats). Tumolo's strikeout rate looks better than Taveras's, but 88 at-bats is variance, not a baseline. It cannot say whether Taveras's 2041 is ordinary for an Athletics second baseman. The comparison is unavailable, not favorable. Blank cells No park, league or run-environment context is on file for any season. Batted-ball, pitch-type and swing data are blank. The box-score line alone cannot say why the rates changed. The dossier has no second 2041 sample for Taveras, such as a split by month or opponent. The latest feed line, off-season, reads 3 EP, 20 PTS, 1170 CR, 5th. That is not a batting measure, and this memo does not use it.

The claim Taveras's 2041 home-run rate (one every 10.3 at-bats) and strikeout rate (one every 6.9 at-bats) are both outside the range of his six prior seasons. The record cannot yet separate a lasting change from one season at the extreme end. His six earlier lines point toward the outlier reading. One 555-at-bat season is enough to establish an event, but it is not enough to establish an identity. What would kill it Take 2042 with at least 500 at-bats. If Taveras hits a home run no less often than once every 16.3 at-bats, the pace of his best pre-2041 season, and strikes out no more often than once every 4.9 at-bats, the outlier reading fails. In that case 2041 would be the start of a new range. If his home-run rate falls back past once every 20 at-bats, it was an outlier. If it lands between those two marks, the dossier still cannot decide, and the memo says so. Earlier Tribune coverage in C84 recorded the $225 million commitment to Taveras, and C110 listed him as the club's second baseman. The 2041 line is the first season on the dossier that meets the pay.

We are all just trying to stay focused and keep pushing through, and it is awesome to see the community’s energy behind us. My wife loves seeing the wins too. They are answering with the same three straight nights of staying past the final horn, the same low growl that used to mean frustration now meaning something else. The front office can call it whatever they want in the next press release. The city already answered. We are not done waiting. We are just done pretending the wait is the story.

Who Owns KONO's Rent Pressure When Everyone on Telegraph Says Business Is Good? By Jax Caldera, The Bay Tribune Priya Raghunathan was feeding quarters into a dryer on Telegraph when I asked her about decay. She dispatches rail for BART and lives in KONO. She looked at me like I'd asked about a plague. "I've noticed that KONO is getting busier. Retail is busy and events are drawing crowds. We're also getting new households moving into the neighborhood." Dmitri Soto runs a container yard, lives in KONO, and was folding towels two machines down. He heard the question and didn't wait for me to finish. "I haven't really seen any decay around here. KONO's been bustling, to be honest. Retail's busy, events are drawing crowds, and we're getting new households moving in. It's all pretty positive from where I'm standing."

My read, and it's inference, is that they don't contradict each other the way they look like they do. Look at what Priya and Dmitri are celebrating: new households moving in. Then look at the housing pressure number. The map has the median rent in KONO at $2,062. A neighborhood can be loud, full and bleeding at once. Busy retail doesn't tell you who gets to stay. The audit's own finding is the part that burns. No active initiative, and no mitigator, owns this break on the record. I checked the running list of what the city says it's working on. Stabilization is paying out in West Oakland. A transit hub is in design in Fruitvale. Grand Lake has a commercial vote ready. KONO's name isn't on any of it.

I can't answer that. The prior comparison the audit needs to validate its own direction isn't in my hands. Nobody at any office has answered the mismatch, either. I also called a waiter who works in San Antonio, not KONO. Dank Abara is the only person I reached who said the word out loud. "I've heard people talking about KONO neighborhood decay, and to be honest, it's something that's on my mind," he said. "I just know that around here, people are talking about it." He admits he doesn't know the specifics. Neither do I. But when a neighborhood with a "growth" label gets talked about as decaying by people one neighborhood over, that's a rumor with a reason behind it. The rumor is a rent number nobody is watching.

The Name Nobody Said in Uptown By Ines Sorensen, The Bay Tribune "I keep looking at the board and seeing the same three names." Priya Narang wrote that on her own page after work this cycle. She directs EMS and lives in Uptown. "Yu Zen's burns, Deacon's hand, Maurice's lungs—none of them should have happened if the systems worked the way they're supposed to. But they didn't, and I'm the one who has to answer for that when the next shift comes in. Ariana's chart is still on my desk, and I don't know why I haven't filed it away yet. Some days the paperwork is the only thing that tells you what you actually did, and I'm not sure I want to read it."

I went to Uptown this cycle to ask about the A's trade of Carmen Mesa. Her page doesn't say his name. It hasn't for weeks. The same three names have sat on her board since the paper's C113 pages. The paper's C93 coverage had Mesa throwing nine scoreless innings in his debut, a twenty-two-year-old out of Midland. I was braced for Uptown to have something to say about him. I read the pages Uptown has given me, and nobody there says his name. Narang's other line, the one she gave a reporter, is about the team. "The A's winning season really brings Uptown together. When they're doing well, the whole neighborhood feels it. The bars and galleries stay packed, and you can feel the energy."

Omar Amici is a construction laborer who lives on the same side of Uptown. The paper carried his words in C113 and C114, and he hasn't changed them. "To be honest, the changes in Uptown have me feeling a bit uneasy. The streets are busier than ever, and it seems like every other place is a for-rent sign these days." On his page for C113 he carried a question of his own. "Why does this change feel different from the others I've already watched happen here?" Ingmar Jordan is a spoken word poet in Uptown, and he was asked about the neighborhood too. "To be honest, I've lost on the UNDOCKED book, but it's not really on my mind when I'm thinking about the neighborhood changes." His own page, from C114, holds a question. "What exactly is changing in my neighborhood, and how do I feel about it?" Three people in one neighborhood were asked about the same team, and each answered about the block. I don't know what Uptown makes of Mesa. I can't hear it on these pages. The only page on the roster that carries his first name belongs to a man across town. Pablo Almanzar pitches for the A's and lives in Chinatown. His page, from C114, holds this question: "Will the front office sort out the roster, and what happens to Carmen's spot and mine?"

1. Carmen Mesa’s Actual Roster Arc: The Emergency Call-Up, Not a Trade The Call-Up (Cycle 91): When number-two starter Henry Rivas suffered a dislocated right shoulder early in the season, General Manager Mike Paulson and manager Deacon Seymour chose not to trade for an outside veteran [188–189, 321–322, 342]. Instead, they summoned 21-year-old Cuban right-hander Carmen Mesa (POP-00081) from the Double-A Midland RockHounds [1-4]. The Dominant Fill-In: In his major-league debut against the Chicago Cubs, Mesa tossed a complete-game shutout with twelve strikeouts [5, 6]. Across his first two starts (15.1 innings), he struck out twenty-two batters while allowing just one earned run [2, 5]. The Option Down (Cycle 98): When Rivas was medically cleared in Cycle 98 and tossed seven shutout innings against the Kansas City Royals, Mesa was optioned back down to the minor leagues (Midland/Triple-A) [190, 398–399]. As The Bay Tribune noted, optioning Mesa was a reward for holding the rotation slot steady, keeping him first in line for roster expansion rather than relinquishing his contract rights [7].

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 2. The Reaction Along Uptown and Telegraph Avenue to Mesa While Mesa was never dealt away, his brief, electric stint sparked immediate debate in the neighborhood: The Telegraph Avenue Barroom Chatter: In the sports lounges and taprooms along Telegraph Avenue (the commercial corridor linking Uptown and KONO) and down to the Jack London waterfront, Mesa’s strikeout rate set the neighborhood buzzing [2]. The Rivas Debate: Patrons openly argued whether veteran starter Henry Rivas had been "superseded by tomorrow" [2]. When Mesa was optioned without drama upon Rivas's return, the reaction along Telegraph was not outrage over a trade, but an appreciation of the front office's organizational pitching depth [189–190, 399].

civic_c115_noah-tan_packet-v2_x-ai-grok-4-3.staged.md By Noah Tan, The Bay Tribune Ramon Vega stood on the same West Oakland block where the new bench had gone in the day before. The pine boards had already lost their raw scent to the air. Two folding chairs remained at the curb across the street, their occupants still talking as the light held. A third person had joined them, coat draped over one arm, listening without hurry. Vega watched the exchange lengthen past the usual quick nod and pass-by.

He stepped closer to the bench, ran a hand along the backrest, and turned toward the open storefront. “Mild doesn't have to mean weak — I still believe that,” he said. “Five days of this clear, easy weather and you see it everywhere: people sitting longer on the benches, kids staying out after the tutoring program lets go, neighbors actually talking to each other instead of rushing past. That's not weakness. That's the city catching its breath. And the work still gets done — the council business, the follow-through, the fights worth having. I've just learned that you don't have to shout to be heard. Sometimes you show up steady, you listen, and you move the bench. That's still how I see it.”

Clarissa Dane and Isaac Martinez, talking Clarissa Dane: Isaac, I've spent enough time walking these blocks to know that the empty storefronts aren't just eyesores — they're a signal. This initiative keeps the landlords who held the line on rent in place instead of letting another wave of displacement hollow out Grand Lake or West Oakland. We've watched what happens when we don't anchor these spaces: the community loses its footing, and the people who've held on get priced out. That's why I'm backing it.

Isaac Martinez: I hear you on the empty storefronts. I walk past three of them every day on my way to a job, and yeah, they're a drag on the whole block. But I gotta ask — what's this actually doing for the folks who are already here? My neighbor's been fighting a rent hike for six months, and I don't see how keeping a landlord in place helps her out. If the money's going to hold the line on rent, great. If it's just keeping the building from changing hands, that's a different story. Clarissa Dane: That's the right question, and here's the concrete part: the stabilization fund isn't just about who owns the building, it's about who gets to stay in it. When a landlord holds the line on rent instead of flipping the property, your neighbor's fight doesn't start over with a new owner who wants market rate the day they close. It keeps the pressure off her while we work the housing side, and it keeps the block from turning over so fast that nobody has a chance to organize.

Isaac Martinez: I get that, and I won't pretend stability isn't worth something. But I've seen this before — a landlord "holding the line" until the pressure's off, then selling to the highest bidder anyway. My buddy Mateo's whole building got flipped two years ago, and every tenant had to move in under three months. If this fund's got teeth, if it actually locks the rent for years, not just a cycle or two, then I'm with you. If it's just a band-aid, we're all just waiting for the next shoe to drop.

West Oakland, in their own words P Slayer — Journalist, Fan Columnist - Sports It's the sandwich board outside the corner store—the one that's been leaning crooked for a week now, advertising "FRESH COLD DRINKS" in letters that are peeling. Every time I walk past it, I straighten it. Every time, it's crooked again by the next morning. I know it's not about the board. It's about wanting one thing in this neighborhood to stay where I put it, when half the block is changing hands and nothing feels fixed. But honestly? I'm just tired. I've been running on coffee and adrenaline for three cycles, chasing the next story, the next climb, the next thing that'll make the place feel like mine. That board doesn't matter. The fact that I keep fixing it does.

Downtown, in their own words Adash Stanley — PG / The Oaks The energy around the Oaks is electric. I've felt it building, and it's like the whole city is waking up with the team. KONO, in their own words Briar Soto — Electrician The A's sent Mesa away, and I keep circling back to it. He threw that shutout against the Cubs, and I was there, yelling so loud my kid covered his ears. And now he's gone because they had Rivas and Almanzar and no room for a guy who just needed a chance. It's not really about Mesa, though. It's that I know what it's like to be good at something and have the numbers not work out — you do the job right, wire everything clean, and the invoice still comes back short. I don't know how to explain that to anyone. So I just sit here and feel annoyed about a baseball player, because it's easier than thinking about my own books.
